newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Court upholds UBS plan for single share.
newsitem.headline: Court upholds UBS plan for single share.

text.p: Union Bank of Switzerland (UBS) on Thursday won another victory in its long-standing battle with financier Martin Ebner as Zurich's Commercial Court dismissed a suit blocking the introduction of a single share.
The court confirmed that a decision by UBS shareholders in November 1994 to launch a single share was legal and the bank said it hoped to introduce the single shares very soon.
"If BK Vision doesn't appeal, then it is all over and we intend to introduce a single share immediately," a UBS spokeswoman said in response to inquiries.

Ebner, who chairs the BK Vision investment trust, have been in an argument over corporate governance for years, but matters came to a head in 1994 when UBS decided to change its share structure, effectively drastically reducing the voting power of BK Vision, UBS's largest shareholder.
Following the decision to introduce the single share, BK Vision and lawyer Peter Hafter filed suits alleging wrongdoing, thus preventing the decision from taking effect.
BK Vision and Hafter have 30 days to appeal the decision.
In addition to the two suits calling for annulment, BK Vision has filed suit, alleging criminal charges against UBS management and a civil suit against the board of directors.
The UBS spokeswoman, however, said these other suits do not affect the decision to introduce a single share.
UBS said the court had dismissed in their entirety the two actions brought by BK Vision and Hafter.

"UBS is extremely satisfied that there is a clear and substantial decision in the important conflict over the introduction a unitary share. UBS hopes to be able to introduce the unitary share as soon as possible," UBS said.
The court confirmed UBS was correct in the way it acted regarding proxy voting rights and confirmed it had the right to vote the shares in its custody for which it was given proxy.
The court also examined the issue of voting rights attached to shares bought on a forward basis.
"It is very positive that in the well-known Kipp case the court said we acted correctly and the deal was done at market prices," the UBS spokeswoman said.

The main issue in BK Vision's action for annulment was whether shares bought by a UBS subsidiary from Karl Heinz Kipp -- a wealthy German living in Switzerland -- on a forward basis for delivery after the shareholders' meeting could be voted by Kipp.
The court ruled that there was no proof of an agreement of how to vote at the shareholders' meeting and the owner of the shares, Kipp, was therefore entitled to vote.
"The person who is a shareholder at the time of the shareholders' meeting is entitled to vote," UBS said.
